title: What hypothesis testing is: the null and alternative hypotheses
summary: Hypothesis testing as a formal way to judge a claim about a population parameter, the null (H0) and alternative (H1 or Ha) hypotheses, and the flour package and market share examples.

chunks.heading: Hypothesis testing in one line
chunks.explanation_md:
**Hypothesis testing** is a **formal method to decide if there is enough evidence to support a claim about a population parameter**.

It always sets up **two competing statements**:
- the **null hypothesis (H0)**, and
- the **alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha)**.

You then look at **sample data** and make one of only two decisions: **reject H0** or **fail to reject H0**.

Notice the second option is *fail to reject*, not *accept*. You will see why in the legal system comparison later in this module.

chunks.heading: Null versus alternative
chunks.explanation_md:
**Null hypothesis (H0):** the **default assumption**. It says there is **no effect or no difference**, and it is **often a statement of equality**.

**Alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha):** the **outcome you seek to support**, that is, **there is an effect or a difference**. It **can be two-sided or one-sided**.

A quick way to remember it: H0 is the boring "nothing has changed" story. Ha is the claim you actually want evidence for.

chunks.heading: Example: flour packages that should weigh 40 ounces
chunks.explanation_md:
Flour is sold by weight, and a particular package size is **supposed to average 40 ounces**.

- **H0:** the average weight of the packages **is 40 ounces** (no problem).
- **H1:** the average **is not 40 ounces** (the **process is out of control**).

In symbols:

**H0: μ = 40 oz**

**H1: μ ≠ 40 oz**

H0 holds the equality, exactly as the definition says. H1 uses **≠**, so it is two-sided: too light or too heavy both count as a problem.

chunks.heading: Example: a market share above 18%
chunks.explanation_md:
A company has **held an 18% share of the market**. After an **increased marketing effort**, officials **believe the share is now greater than 18%** and want to prove it.

Here the parameter is the **market share p**, written as a decimal (18% is 0.18).

**H0: p ≤ 0.18**

**H1: p > 0.18**

The claim the officials want to prove (greater than 18%) goes into **H1**. Everything else, including the equality, stays in **H0**. Because H1 points in one direction, this is a one-sided alternative.

questions.stem: Differentiate between the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis.
questions.model_answer_md:
Every hypothesis test sets up two competing statements about a population parameter.

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** the **default assumption**, saying there is **no effect or no difference**. It is **often a statement of equality**.
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha):** the **outcome you seek to support**, saying there **is an effect or a difference**. It **can be two-sided or one-sided**.
- **Decision:** based on sample data we either **reject H0** or **fail to reject H0**.
- **Example:** for flour packages meant to average 40 ounces, H0: μ = 40 oz (no problem) and H1: μ ≠ 40 oz (process out of control).

So H0 is the status quo, and Ha is the claim that needs evidence.

questions.stem: Define hypothesis testing and state the two decisions it can lead to.
questions.model_answer_md:
Hypothesis testing is how a researcher checks a claim using sample data.

- **Definition:** a **formal method to decide if there is enough evidence to support a claim about a population parameter**.
- **Two statements:** it involves the **null hypothesis (H0)** and the **alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha)**.
- **Two decisions:** based on **sample data**, we either **reject H0** or **fail to reject H0**.

The test never proves H0; it only asks whether the evidence is strong enough to reject it.

Two competing statements: H0 and H1 or Ha
Decision: reject H0 or fail to reject H0

questions.stem: A company has held an 18% share of the market. After an increased marketing effort, officials believe the share is now greater than 18%. Write the null and alternative hypotheses and explain your choice.
questions.model_answer_md:
The claim the officials want to prove decides where each statement goes.

- **Parameter:** the market share **p**, written as a decimal, so 18% = **0.18**.
- **Alternative (the claim):** the share is now **greater than 18%**, so **H1: p > 0.18**.
- **Null (everything else, including equality):** **H0: p ≤ 0.18**.
- **Type:** because H1 points in **one direction**, this is a **one-sided** alternative.

The claim to be proved goes into H1, and the null keeps the equality.

questions.stem: What is hypothesis testing? Explain the null and alternative hypotheses, and illustrate with the flour package and market share examples.
questions.model_answer_md:
Hypothesis testing lets a business researcher use sample data to check a claim instead of relying on opinion.

**Meaning:** a **formal method to decide if there is enough evidence to support a claim about a population parameter**. It sets up **two competing statements**, and based on **sample data** we either **reject H0** or **fail to reject H0**.

**Null hypothesis (H0):** the **default assumption**: **no effect or no difference**, **often a statement of equality**.

**Alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha):** the **outcome you seek to support**: there **is an effect or a difference**. It can be:
- **two-sided**, Ha: parameter ≠ value, used when any deviation matters;
- **one-sided**, Ha: parameter > value or < value, used when the direction matters.

**Example 1: flour packages (two-sided).** A package size is supposed to average **40 ounces**.
- H0: μ = 40 oz (no problem)
- H1: μ ≠ 40 oz (the process is out of control)
Too light or too heavy are both problems, so H1 uses ≠.

**Example 2: market share (one-sided).** A company has held an **18%** share; after an increased marketing effort, officials believe it is now **greater than 18%** and want to prove it.
- H0: p ≤ 0.18
- H1: p > 0.18
The claim to be proved goes into H1, and the equality stays with H0.

**Conclusion:** H0 is the status quo that stands unless the data argue strongly against it, and H1 is the claim the researcher needs evidence for.

Reject or fail to reject H0 based on sample data
H0: default, no effect, equality; Ha: effect or difference
Two-sided vs one-sided alternatives
Flour: H0 μ = 40 oz, H1 μ ≠ 40 oz
Market share: H0 p ≤ 0.18, H1 p > 0.18

questions.stem: Using the flour and market share examples, distinguish between a two-sided and a one-sided alternative hypothesis. How does the choice affect where the rejection region lies?
questions.model_answer_md:
The alternative hypothesis can be two-sided or one-sided, and this decides how the test is set up.

**Two-sided (non-directional) alternative:**
- Form: **Ha: parameter ≠ value**; used when we **care about any deviation** from the value.
- **Flour example:** H0: μ = 40 oz, H1: μ ≠ 40 oz. A package that is too light or too heavy means the process is out of control.
- **Rejection region:** divided into **two tails** of the distribution. At α = .05 the slide's picture puts **.025 in each tail**, beyond **Z = -1.96 and Z = 1.96**.

**One-sided (directional) alternative:**
- Form: **Ha: parameter > value** or **Ha: parameter < value**; used when **the direction of the effect matters**.
- **Market share example:** H0: p ≤ 0.18, H1: p > 0.18, because officials want to prove the share has gone **up**.
- **Rejection region:** the **entire probability of an unlikely outcome** sits in the tail named by Ha. The slide's picture puts all of **α = .05 in the right tail**, beyond **Z = 1.645**.

**Conclusion:** the wording of the claim ("not equal" vs "greater than" or "less than") decides whether the rejection region is split across two tails or placed in one.

rubric.point: Two-sided: Ha ≠, any deviation matters
Flour example is two-sided
Two tails, .025 each, beyond ±1.96
One-sided: Ha > or <, direction matters
Market share example is one-sided (p > 0.18)
All of α = .05 in one tail beyond 1.645
